resources.string: How light becomes a visual signal
Simplified visual pathway. Light rays and signals are slowed for illustration. This is not an eye test or a prescription.
How rods and cones share vision
Brightness, color and the number of dots are illustrative. Display settings affect this animation; it cannot measure sensitivity or color vision.
Light bends at the cornea, then passes through the pupil. The iris adjusts the size of this opening to control how much light enters.
Light is focused on the retina
The cornea and lens bend light so that an image can focus on the retina. The lens can change shape to help focus at different distances.
In a rod, light activates rhodopsin and starts a chain that lowers cGMP. Ion channels close, the cell gets more negative inside, and it releases less glutamate.
In this simplified cone route, a cone signals to a bipolar cell and then a ganglion cell. Light moves toward the outer retina; the relay runs back toward the inner retina.
Axons of retinal ganglion cells form the optic nerve. Some fibers cross, and signals relay through the thalamus before reaching the visual cortex.
As the scene gets darker, fine detail and colors become harder to see. Vision does not switch instantly from cones to rods.
Rods gain sensitivity in the dark
In very dim light, rods become the main source of vision after adapting. They help detect shapes and motion but do not provide color vision.
At intermediate light levels, both rods and cones contribute. How much each contributes depends on the light and the part of the retina being used.
Cones support detail in bright light
In bright light, cones support fine detail. They are especially dense at the central fovea, where we see sharpest.
Cone signals combine to support color
Three cone classes have overlapping sensitivities to different wavelengths. The brain compares their signals; one cone alone does not identify a color.
